question: What is the meaning of unusual consumption in relation to interactive decision support tools (tools that support exploration and decision-making in ce object governance)?
data_group: interactive decision support tools (tools that support exploration and decision-making in ce object governance)
description: The meaning of unusual consumption in relation to interactive decision support tools (tools that support exploration and decision-making in CE object governance) refers to instances where the consumption patterns or decisions made through these tools deviate significantly from the norm or expected behavior. This could indicate unique or unconventional choices being considered or made during the exploration and decision-making processes related to the governance of circular economy objects.

3.7. Stakeholders 
Since passports are about the governance of the entire product life 
cycle, it may be helpful to understand who the involved actors are, what 
their role is and perspective they hold toward passports. We choose to 
anchor the actor analysis to the most frequently used life cycle variant 
(Stark, 2015, p. 7). This view categorizes the management of a product 
life cycle from the environmental point of view into five phases: (1) raw 
material extraction, (2) manufacturing, (3) transportation, (4) utiliza­
tion (including maintenance), and (5) disposal or recycling. We have 
grouped identified roles based on similar function which resulted in 
twelve actor types that typically interact with a passport (see Fig. 6). 
These roles operate in four distinctive information chains grouped by 
information type: (1) the owners’ chain, (2) the governance chain, (3) 
the financial chain, and (4) the production chain. In the owners’ chain, 
we observe actors that are assigned with the majority of legal re­
sponsibilities for an object, i.e., either by owning it, leasing it or when 
assigned this responsibility from the owner (e.g., facility managers). The 
key objective for these actors is to have access to information that 
support the decision-making regarding the optimal acquiring and 
maintenance of an object according to the needs of the end-user. The 
governance chain is concerned with the task of securing the supply 
system in which the passport is used by verifying the quality, integrity, 
and validity of the information registered in or made accessible by 
passports. In this role of gatekeeper, we typically find the government, 
independent auditors, and passport software providers. The financial 
chain is concerned with financing and insuring an object. The key 
objective is to ensure a correct valuation of an object in order to identify 
the corresponding risk or to determine financing premiums. Finally, the 
production chain is mainly responsible for the physical life cycle oper­
ations performed on the object. This varies from material supply to 
design, production, assembly, distribution, maintenance and disman­
tling activities. The key objective of this group of actors is to document 
their activities in order that others later may benefit from this infor­
mation (including themselves, e.g., in maintenance activities). 
When considering the key opportunities and the key barriers (listed 
unweighted in Table A7, Appendix 5) we observe a misalignment be­
tween the stakes and challenges of different actors; some actors mainly 
benefit while others are charged with data registration and management 
costs. This observation is shared among other studies (e.g., Adisorn et al. 
(2021); Bouwend Nederland (2020); Debacker and Manshoven (2016); 
Greer et al. (2020); Munaro and Tavares (2021)). In some cases, there 
may even be adversarial thoughts against a passport as an information 
gain for one actor may lead to a deterioration of the negotiation position 
of another actor (e.g., recyclers). More generally, the majority of studies 
report that a passport facilitates environmental gains, and often also 
financial gains, hence, observe a societal-cost-benefit business case for 
implementing passports. 
3.8. Goals 
The ’identification of reuse value in the product’ is listed as the 
primary goal of a passport. A major part of this particular goal originates 
from papers related to the BAMB research project (Debacker and 
Manshoven, 2016), but it is used also extensively in direct phrasing or 
similar wording in other projects (Bertino et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019; 
Merrild et al., 2016; Wittenveen & Bos, 2018).

human actors to resources. The environmental impact module catego­
rizes stages of activities, from raw material extraction to disposal, as 
‘Events’, with a focus on tracking their environmental impact. Addi­
tionally, the ‘Spatiotemporal Extent’ pattern adds granularity to the 
‘Event’ pattern by making it possible to model the spatial and temporal 
trajectory of an event over time and space. This pattern is particularly 
useful for detailing carbon emissions, water usage, or energy con­
sumption at different stages and locations of an event, answering 
questions such as: What is the energy consumption in different stages of 
a product production? What is the carbon emission rate at different 
geographical points and times during the manufacturing phase of a 
product? To leverage the full capabilities of the ‘Events’ and ‘Spatio­
temporal Extent’, we defined our Environmental Impact module as a 
subclass of the ‘Events’ pattern (see supplementary information S6). 
The “Quantities and Units” pattern quantifies various attributes of 
environmental impacts of different Events, such as water footprint, 
carbon footprint, and energy consumption, and associates them with 
specific events or spatiotemporal extents. However, instead of directly 
assigning a float, integer, or string value to these properties as datatype 
properties, we introduced classes as a subclass of ‘Quantity’; for example, 
‘WaterFootprintQuantity’. And, for each created subclass of “Quantity”, 
we created an instance of “QuantityKind”. The “QuantityKind” instance 
can represent the kind of measurement (for example, carbon footprint, 
energy consumption) and the “QuantityValue” will capture the quantity 
of the properties. All quantifiable measurements relevant to the envi­
ronment impact module can be modeled by extending this pattern. By 
standardizing how these quantities are expressed, the pattern enables a 
more structured and comparative analysis of environmental data. This 
makes it possible to model important information that can answer 
questions such as: What is the total carbon footprint of a product from 
raw material extraction to consumer use? What is the water usage 
during the production of a product? The schema diagram is found in 
supplementary information S7. 
Furthermore, instances of ‘EnvrinmentalImpact’ can have associated 
provenance data. To track the source of the data, and the ‘Agent’ 
responsible for it, the “EntityWithProvenance” is used. We associate 
‘EnvrinmentalImpact’ with “EntityWithProvenance” through a subclass 
relationship given that most instances have associated data with them 
(see supplementary information S8). 
Putting it all together, the ‘EnvironmentalImpact’ module is presented 
in supplementary information S9. 
In this paper, we have modeled the key notions for ‘Product’, ‘Ma­
terial’ and ‘EnvironmentalImpact’. Following the same approach, the 
modeling for all key notions identified for developing DPPs is done and 
can be found on the GitHub page (Kebede, 2024). 
4.3.3.2. Axiomatizations. Using the schema diagrams as a guide, axioms 
are added to produce the OWL file. Since we are using patterns, the 
axioms associated with the selected patterns are inherently derived from 
those patterns. Focusing on the use case of this study, some adjustments 
and modifications are introduced when utilizing the axioms. The axioms 
are expressed using description logics. In supplementary information 
S10, we highlight a few examples of axioms that are specific to our 
ontology.
